title: I built a compiler + an "honest benchmark" for AI-authored Spine rigs — the interesting part is catching the AI cheating
author: firejune
selftext:
I've seen a few threads here about AI-assisted rigging, so I want to share the angle I've been working from: instead of asking an AI to drive an editor, give it a compiler — and then measure it in a way it can't game.

**rigc** (MIT, `npm i -g spine-rigc`) compiles two small JSON specs — a rig spec and a motion spec — into a Spine 4.3 skeleton, verified by a spine-core round-trip plus \~35 machine assertions. The idea: everything AIs are bad at (format trivia, coordinate conventions, atlas packing) is the compiler's job; everything they're judged on is measured, not eyeballed.

The part I think is actually novel is the **benchmark protocol**:

* The agent gets a written brief + rendered PNG frames of the target animation — never the answer skeleton.
* A forbidden-reading list with teeth: reference exports, transcriptions, previous runs' measures. Read one and the run is unscored.
* `check` renders the candidate back and compares pixels against the frames: MAE over the *reference's* drawn pixels (so drawing big transparent sprites can't shrink your denominator), per-bone-chain error attribution, per-frame motion deltas.
* The scored diff runs **once, at the end**. Its measures derive from the answer, so running it mid-loop and editing after gets the run labeled "bench-assisted" — a different category, not comparable with clean runs.
* Every run is committed with its full loop log, and a web viewer plays any run beside its reference frames.

Results so far (all in the repo, logs included):

* Claude Opus cleared the simple rungs. On a full character (spineboy) it authors the **structure** perfectly — 18/18 bones, name-agnostic tree similarity 1.000 — but **motion fidelity** stalls: worst-chain drift \~14.6 px against a 0.7–3.3 px bar. After three attempts with real levers each time, I froze that rung as a score gate rather than keep rerolling.
* Last week I ran a deliberately weak model (Gemini Flash) through a pilot. It landed a clean scored run in 3 hours unattended: structure identical to Opus name-agnostically, motion about half as good — and every failure was legible from the instruments without trusting a word of the model's self-report. The judge's verdict sheet is committed too.
* Watching the weak model stumble produced `docs/PROMPTING.md` — the six prompt clauses that actually mattered (progress output on search loops, sparse keys instead of per-frame keys, make the agent typecheck its own helpers, …).

What it can't do yet, honestly: meshes/physics/IK compile and validate, but no benchmark run has proven an AI can *author* them well. Motion fidelity on many-joint characters is the open problem.

Repo: [https://github.com/firejune/rigc](https://github.com/firejune/rigc)

I'd genuinely like this community's read on the approach — especially whether the honesty protocol holds up under adversarial reading, and what you'd measure that I'm not.
